label: succession planning and business continuity
overview: Succession planning scenarios require the advisor to navigate deep-seated emotional dynamics while simultaneously protecting the business from existential risk. Stakeholders naturally become polarised during ownership transitions — humans are wired to argue positions that serve their own survival interests. A structured facilitation framework is essential because it secures agreement on how the problem will be broken down before anyone jumps to solutions, which is precisely the point at which defensive and argumentative instincts are triggered. The advisor's role here is facilitation, not advice — letting go of predetermined outcomes and ensuring the right voices are balanced. Global standards provide the structural backbone: ISO 22301 for business continuity, IFAC for value preservation, and OECD principles for family governance.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the succession scenario driven by a planned transition with adequate lead time, an urgent or unexpected departure event, or unresolved family conflict that is blocking progress?
diagnostic_entry.planned_transition: Work through the full Dream Home methodology in sequence. Begin with the digital discovery questionnaire to establish baseline readiness, then conduct separate wish list meetings with incumbents and successors before bringing stakeholders together. A 5-year lead time is global best practice — if the timeline is shorter, identify which steps must be accelerated and what the corresponding risks are.
diagnostic_entry.urgent_or_unexpected_departure: Engage the ISO 22301 dual-track plan immediately. Identify interim replacements for operational continuity while the permanent succession structure is being designed. The emergency sudden departure plan must be activated or created — do not attempt to compress the full planned succession into a crisis timeline.
diagnostic_entry.family_conflict_blocking_progress: Address the psychological layer before the structural one. Use the Ascension Diagram and an overarching metaphor (Dream Home or Climbing Everest) to create a collaborative frame. Conduct wish list meetings separately with each party — never with both together until expectations have been individually mapped and potential conflict points identified. A Family Constitution is the OECD-recommended mechanism for preventing emotional conflict from derailing the process.

materials.name: Succession Quiz — Initial Discovery Questionnaire
materials.summary: Eases the owner into succession by asking them to picture life after the business — hobbies, family time, future income, mental acuity — before any financial or legal hurdle is raised. It works against Role Identification, the loss of self-worth and community status an owner feels on exiting, by helping them build a clear and genuinely appealing vision of what comes next. For the advisor it produces a baseline readiness report before the first formal meeting.
materials.who_when: Business owners at the very beginning of their succession journey — especially those who are hesitant, or struggling to let go of their business identity.
steps: Direct the client to the digital Succession Quiz before any meeting is booked.
Have them answer the preliminary questions on exit timeline, business value, and life after the business.
Prompt the life-after questions deliberately — hobbies, family time, future income, mental acuity — so the vision of the next chapter forms before the hurdles appear.
Generate the private readiness report and read it for three things: their timeline, their successor options, and their financial clarity.
Judge from the answers how much Role Identification is in play, and pace the engagement to it — an owner whose identity is the business needs the vision built before the transaction is discussed.

materials.name: Succession Metaphor — Dream Home Visual Frameworks
materials.summary: Visual slides that reframe a threatening transition as a collaborative build. An Ascension Diagram running bottom-left to top-right gives participants the felt sense of moving upward and improving, while the Dream Home metaphor engages the logical left brain and the conceptual right brain at once. It also repositions the advisor as a facilitator rather than an expert dictating terms, which is what bypasses the argumentative reflex families bring to conflict.
materials.who_when: Multi-stakeholder families or complex transition teams where confirmation bias, conflict or stress is likely to derail planning early.
steps: Open with the Ascension Diagram so stakeholders see the journey as an upward movement rather than a loss.
Introduce the Dream Home metaphor — the family is not dismantling something, they are designing and building something together.
Use the metaphor to engage both halves of the room: the logical case and the conceptual picture, presented together rather than in sequence.
Position yourself explicitly as the facilitator, not the expert handing down terms — the roadmap is about how the problem will be solved, not what the answer is.
Use the non-threatening roadmap to gain agreement on the process itself before any contested content is opened, heading off the instinctive argumentative reaction.

materials.name: Wishes Meeting Template
materials.summary: A structured questionnaire for gathering the qualitative material succession actually turns on — family considerations, financial needs and successor requirements. It makes sure every voice is heard on stewardship versus ownership, fair market compensation, divorce risk and sibling equity, and it lets the advisor capture the incumbents' and the successors' expectations separately so conflict is not triggered prematurely.
materials.who_when: The formal discovery phase, where legal, estate and emotional wish lists must be documented before the transition plan is designed.
steps: Run the questionnaire across all three areas — Family Considerations, Financial Considerations, and Successor Requirements.
Cover the issues families avoid until they explode: stewardship versus outright ownership, fair market compensation, divorce risk, in-laws, disparate sibling roles, and successor competency.
Capture the incumbents' expectations in their own session, in their own words.
Capture the successors' expectations in a separate, identical session.
Keep the two documents apart until the concept meeting — surfacing them too early is what starts the conflict the process exists to avoid.

materials.name: Comprehensive Guide & 6-Step Dream Home Methodology
materials.summary: The orchestrating guide that grounds the emotional facilitation in global standards — ISO 22301 for risk mitigation, IFAC for value preservation, and OECD governance principles — so the plan is defensible as well as agreed. It supplies the 6-step implementation methodology that sequences the other materials, and the Rule of 5: a five-year lead time to pace the engagement and transfer the skills the successor needs.
materials.who_when: Advisors actively managing a transition and structuring the long-term consulting engagement around it.
steps: Step 1 — Initial discovery: send the client to the Succession Quiz and generate the private readiness report before you meet.

Step 2 — The parents' wish list: like an architect taking requirements, hold the first formal meeting with the incumbents using the Wishes Meeting template to capture financial requirements, estate wishes and successor expectations.

Step 3 — The kids' wish list: run the identical exercise with the incoming successors. Where family disharmony already exists, keep this document completely hidden from the parents to prevent premature conflict.

Step 4 — Concept drawings: bring everyone together, place the parents' wishes alongside the successors', and facilitate the discussion on natural constraints and the compromises required to align expectations.

Step 5 — Final design and sign-off: deliver your recommendations on valuation, tax and legal structure; the family reviews the budget, settles its must-haves, and formally signs off the transition design.

Step 6 — Construction begins: implement a secure succession action plan with assigned tasks, sectioning sensitive tasks off from the wider staff to maintain confidentiality, per OECD governance principles.
Pace the whole engagement to the Rule of 5 — a five-year lead time gives room to transfer vital skills through strategic project assignments and to measure the successor against the timeline.

advisor_guidance.facilitation_over_advice: The advisor's greatest mistake in succession planning is acting as the expert who knows the right answer. Succession involves values, family relationships, and emotional legacies that no outsider can fully understand. The role is to establish the framework, chair the discussion, and balance the voices — not to advocate for a particular outcome. Advisors who push too hard for what they think is best destroy the trust that makes agreement possible.
advisor_guidance.separate_before_joining: Never bring the parties together before gathering their individual wish lists separately. Premature joint meetings allow dominant personalities to set the agenda, silence quieter stakeholders, and create defensive positions that are extremely difficult to reverse. Separate meetings first — always.
advisor_guidance.five_years_is_not_optional: The Rule of 5 is global best practice for a reason. Compressed succession timelines are one of the leading causes of failed transitions — successors are underprepared, goodwill erodes during a rushed handover, and the incumbent's knowledge and relationships are not adequately transferred. If the client presents with less than five years, name the risk explicitly and document it.
advisor_guidance.dual_track_must_exist: The planned transition plan and the emergency departure plan are not alternatives — both must be designed and operational simultaneously. A business that only has a long-term succession plan and loses its key person unexpectedly has no plan at all. The emergency plan must have named interim replacements, pre-defined trigger events, and a clear activation protocol.
advisor_guidance.family_constitution_prevents_legal_dispu: Many succession conflicts that end up in litigation began as disagreements that could have been resolved by objective, pre-agreed family rules. A Family Constitution is not a legal document — it is a governance agreement. Its value is in creating a shared framework for decision-making before the emotional stakes are at their highest.
